paragraphs: Norway has nothing. Apart from its harsh terrain and climate and the North Sea oil fields, there is almost nothing. There are hardly any people. There is no Uniqlo and no Muji. Trondheim in particular is the third largest city in the country, yet there is nothing but the university. But it has appeal. Norwegians have a strong sense of independence and love their country. People come from all over the world to visit or settle. I thought that understanding that gap might lead to understanding Norway itself and its healthcare. With that thought I left Japan.

The university hospital is called St. Olav's Hospital, after a saint in local history. The area this hospital covers is a region called Trondelag County. Do not underestimate it for being a county: it covers about a quarter of the area of the country in central Norway. For this study abroad, I went alone from Nagoya University. I was looked after for one month each in neurology and orthopedics.

In neurology I learned the work on the ward and in the outpatient clinic. What surprised me first was how short the patients' hospital stays are. Hospital stays in Norway are very short, and most patients stayed within a week. I felt as if I had received a baptism, thinking that this is what healthcare in which the state pays the entire medical cost is like. What was especially memorable on the ward was the scene of telling a patient suspected of multiple sclerosis (MS). The patient, a biologist, presumably knew the gravity of it. She was in tears. The doctor repeated, "I understand..." That an attitude of understanding and empathy is important was common to every country. After that a lumbar puncture was to be performed, and it was done without anesthesia. In Norway this is normal, and the doctor in charge told me afterward that he had never used local anesthesia and did not even know why it would be needed. In Japan one sometimes hears "because patients are customers," but during the clerkship at the university hospital I almost never felt that. Here, however, I keenly felt the meaning of those words. In the outpatient clinic I observed Huntington's disease, which is common in Europe and America, and multiple sclerosis, which is especially common in Northern Europe. When it comes to Huntington's disease one thinks of choreiform movements, but in the early stage irritability and constructional apraxia are apparently prominent. Owning a hunting rifle is fairly popular in Norway, but if irritability and the like are observed, I was told the doctor must suspend the person's qualification to own a rifle. For the test of constructional apraxia, besides drawing, they performed a test called Luria's test, which I had never seen in Japan. As for multiple sclerosis, I was told that clinical trials using anti-CD20 antibodies are advancing across Northern Europe. I was also allowed to attend a drug briefing session. Through lumbar puncture and Luria's test, I realized that the "outline of treatment," what test items to check and what treatment to give for a patient, does not differ between Japan and Norway, but I learned that differences between countries appear in how it is done. Another thing I noticed is the advance of gender equality. For example, the ambulance crews. It is recognized as a tough job requiring not only knowledge but also physical and mental strength. My impression is that there are many men in Japan, but there women, if anything, are the majority. The neurology department too had slightly more women, and on some days at the morning conference all nine people other than me were women.

The next month I was looked after in orthopedics. Orthopedics was more like a group of craftsmen, and at first I was confused about whom to rely on, but I somehow succeeded in conveying my wishes and was assigned to the trauma group in the first week and the joint replacement group in the second week. In the third week, after consulting with that doctor, I was assigned to the hand surgery group, which has many operations. First I staked out the waiting room of the operating suite and succeeded in making friends with the nurses who manage the operating rooms and the scrub nurses. There was a reason I came to communicate with nurses rather than doctors. It is because the surgeon does not enter the room until entry, induction of anesthesia, and fixation of the limbs are finished. Conversely, as soon as the surgeon entered, after confirming with the surrounding staff the status of anesthesia, preparation of instruments, antibiotics and so on, he started the incision three minutes after entering the room. It is truly efficient work. Incidentally, there is usually only one surgeon. As for anesthesia, although the anesthesiologist does the induction, maintenance and emergence are done by anesthesia nurses. The anesthesia nurse system is a system characteristic of the Nordic countries, and one can obtain the qualification by training for one and a half years after obtaining a nursing license. After induction, the anesthesiologist apparently remotely monitors several operating rooms from another room. Personnel costs are also 100% state-funded, so they must be reduced. In anesthesia, I was told, personnel costs are reduced in this way. For joint replacement operations there is an anteroom, and there the anesthesia nurse performed spinal block, sedation, securing intravenous access and insertion of a urinary catheter. In this way they raise the turnover rate of the operating rooms. I thought the bed would be transferred and transported, but looking closely, the bed in the anteroom was also a mobile operating table. It moved as it was to the operating room, and at the same time the surgeon entered, and the incision began three minutes later. I felt that efficiency taken this far is even artistic.

I summarized what I learned in the following three points. First, the content of medical care does not differ between Japan and Norway, but how it is carried out differs greatly. When a patient comes to the hospital, the test items and treatment content are roughly the same even in different countries. This is thanks to the development of worldwide guidelines and to papers published in English and the systems for publishing and searching them. I keenly felt the importance of updating medical knowledge. And conversely, a big difference arose in how tests and treatments are carried out. This depends greatly on region, culture and custom, and further on the healthcare system and ways of working described below. Second, Norwegians value their working environment, and this is due to a fundamental and latent strategy of the people of this country. That is because Norway has almost the same area as Japan but only one twenty-fifth of Japan's population. In addition, it is full of factors that lead people toward depression, such as the polar night and the cold. Therefore, as a labor force, an awareness of cherishing one another works among the people. That means keeping working hours moderate and enriching life, so that everyone lives healthily and contributes to society. Hence people seek efficiency. Third, the purpose of a doctor's work changes greatly depending on the healthcare system. Specialists at large hospitals in Norway devote themselves, as specialists, to diagnosis, to setting treatment policy, or to surgery, and promptly request transfer or follow-up for chronic-phase treatment and maintenance to GPs, rehabilitation hospitals, facilities for the elderly and so on. Norwegian doctors, while saying that this is treatment that strains the national treasury, do not worry about income and expenditure and do not hesitate to give the best care to patients who need it. Patients who do not need treatment are sent home right away. I got a sense that it is close to the original form of acute care.

I thought that people generally consider that accumulated history, culture and achievements lead to authority. All of these are wonderful, but when authority goes too far it invites the fixing of hierarchy and stagnation of communication. NTNU is a university that boasts a history of several hundred years as a university itself, but in Norway I felt that people do not cling to things like authority, and that each works with confidence and pride in themselves. I too felt a liking for that.

On site I was looked after by Dr. M, a Japanese PhD. After finishing initial residency at Nagoya University Hospital, Dr. M works as a PhD in the epidemiology division at NTNU. Besides giving me advice about life in Norway by phone even before I left Japan, after I arrived in Trondheim he also invited me to his workplace, his home and even a bouldering gym. I was also looked after by Dr. H, a Japanese neurosurgeon. He is a doctor in the field of functional neurosurgery, specifically specializing in treatments by insertion of electrodes, such as spinal cord stimulation (SCS) for chronic pain and deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the brain for tremor in Parkinson's disease and so on. He invited me to his operations.

For giving me this opportunity in this study abroad, I sincerely thank everyone at NTNU and St. Olav's Hospital, Dr. H and Dr. M in Trondheim, and many doctors, starting with Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 of the International Collaboration Office of Nagoya University. Thank you very much.
